tradition.name: Dark Progressive House
tradition.lineage: Dark progressive house — brooding, harmonically layered house associated with extended DJ development.

extras.description: Dark progressive house emphasizes shadowy atmosphere, gradual builds and intricate harmonic layers over a steady house pulse. Its DJs and producers develop long transitions and evolving textures, connecting progressive-house structure with a darker, immersive club sound. Moshic and related radio and label communities illustrate this strand.
exemplars: Moshic — complete January2022 live DJ mix1:00:26

tradition.name: Anime Rap
tradition.lineage: Anime rap — fan-created hip-hop interpreting anime characters, stories and worlds.

extras.description: Anime rap turns characters and storylines from Japanese animation into original rap narratives. Performers combine rhythmic verses, hooks and produced hip-hop beats with fan interpretation, sometimes speaking through a character’s perspective. Online video communities support a transnational field that overlaps nerdcore and rap geek while centering anime themes.
exemplars: Juu Rafaela and Hawky — complete O Fim do Clã Zenin (Acapella),2026

tradition.name: Armenian Hip Hop
tradition.lineage: Armenian hip hop connects rap production in Armenia and its diaspora, including work concerned with cultural memory, social experience and contemporary life. Diaspora artists also draw on the wider hip-hop scenes in which they work.

extras.description: Rhythmic verses, storytelling and wordplay interact with produced beats and, in some songs, sung hooks. Boom-bap-influenced production and unaccompanied protest delivery are among the approaches used within the field.

entries.geo_rationale: Documented White House protest locality; Washington anchor for the selected diaspora performance, not a national origin claim.
entries.neighbor_distinction: Armenian hip hop is a national and diaspora hip-hop cultural field, not a translation of Armenian folk or all Armenian music. The community-run ArmenianDC programme positively places Marc’s hip-hop work and Armenian historical narrative within its Armenian cultural calendar; the first-person account documents actual genocide-commemoration practice, rather than inferring musical identity from ancestry alone. Existing conscious_hip_hop overlaps substantially in political narrative and lyrical craft and is not confined to its sample-based exemplar, but spans many communities rather than the Armenian national/diaspora field. Existing armenian_traditional, armenian_folk and armenian_duduk_chant cover liturgical, folk, ashugh and ceremonial traditions; commemorative subject matter alone does not make rap those practices. Armenian pop and Armenian indie overlap the national community but have popular-song/indie field scopes, not all Armenian rap. The selected English-language diaspora branch does not imply Armenian-language exclusivity, all performers living in Armenia, or that all Armenian rap is protest rap. Neither the unrelated Gulf traditions nor a presumed world-rap umbrella is claimed as an equivalent; no separate world_rap or gulf_hip_hop entry was found in the current loader. Current old records and queued038 corpus checked; no matching Armenian rap candidate found. Exact creator map retrieval failed, so membership is not asserted; positive first-person practice plus Armenian community presentation support this category.

These beats circulate as standalone releases as well as potential settings for rap.

tradition.name: Detroit Trap Brasileiro
tradition.lineage: Detroit trap brasileiro — Brazil’s early-2020s adaptation of Detroit rap, marked by punchline-led Portuguese verses, loose placement against the beat and prominent rhythmic bass.

extras.description: Detroit trap brasileiro adapts Detroit rap’s playful punchlines and elastic delivery to Brazilian Portuguese. Piano figures, prominent bass and buoyant percussion frame loosely placed verses, often with irreverent humor. The scene expanded in the early 2020s through independent rappers and producers, with sampling and local references giving the imported style new inflections.

entries.neighbor_distinction: Existing Trap Brasileiro describes the broad Atlanta-derived national trap field. This requested field is its specifically Detroit-influenced branch, positively identified in original Brazilian scene criticism through timing, punchline emphasis and production habits. Existing Detroit Hip Hop already includes later Detroit rappers, so no claim that its scope ends with Dilla; the Brazilian Portuguese producer/rapper network and documented adaptation are the distinction. Detroit Techno/House are separate dance-music lineages. Overlap with broader trap is explicit, not evidence of an exact alias.
entries.model_policy: Genre-level representative piano-driven rap arrangement, not a reconstruction of an individual master. Original specialist scene analysis describes drums, prominent bass and guiding piano as characteristic production roles; an authored 808-style percussion/bass engine and repeating concert-grand piano motif retain these roles. The original physical piano, software, sample source and synthesizer architecture are not asserted. Sample-based alternatives exist, but this keyboard-played rendition is not a claim to reproduce their embedded audio. One rhythmic spoken lead, moderate effort, short repeated piano cells and controlled studio capture are authored choices. The current controls do not specify the source’s measured off-grid timing; no exact flow-delay claim. A coherent standard concert-grand timbre gives the piano motif a clear low-register foundation alongside the drum/bass engine; this is an authored production timbre, not a claim that a physical concert grand appeared on the source recordings.
entries.source_scope_limitation: Representative genre practice; no claim every track uses piano, every bass is808, or exact measured vocal timing. Source models/headcounts unknown.

tradition.name: Ethiopian Hip Hop
tradition.lineage: Ethiopian rap developed through Addis Ababa and diaspora networks, adapting hip-hop rhythms to Amharic and other local languages.

extras.description: Ethiopian hip hop combines rhythmic rap with produced beats and local language wordplay. Amharic is prominent alongside Oromo, Tigrinya and English, with themes ranging from everyday life and storytelling to social criticism. Addis Ababa artists and diaspora collaborators connect boom-bap and trap production with Ethiopian cultural references.

tradition.name: German Viral Rap
tradition.lineage: A German-language rap community shaped by online video creators, collaborations and rapidly circulating songs. Music, comedy, gaming and choreographed video production intersect within the broader Deutschrap field.

extras.description: Rhythmic German-language delivery and memorable refrains ride programmed beats and a defined electronic low end. Vocal character, punchlines and contrasts between rap passages and hooks work closely with the visual presentation, while production draws on contemporary rap and pop.

entries.geo_rationale: Country-level editorial anchor for positively documented German video-creator discovery community, not arranger location or claimed recording venue.
entries.neighbor_distinction: German Viral Rap identifies the German-language video-creator rap discovery community. Exact creator corpus includes Julien Bam, Rezo, Standart Skill, Lukas Der Rapper, Arazhul, ApoRed, gaming songs and creator collaborations; Julien Bam is positively listed. PopNRW institutional artist profile documents music-video production, a specific internet music-video hype and creator collaborations; his own site establishes the combined music/comedy/video practice. German Deutschrap already spans historical and contemporary streaming-dominant rap, not only its early exemplars; this is a narrower creator-production and circulation network within that broad field. Meme Rap already includes internet circulation and comic performance, and Comedy Rap includes comic character/parody as organizing purpose: both overlap substantially, while neither specifies this German-language creator network. German Pop is broad despite its selected songwriter branch; German Hyperpop is a distinct internet-generation sonic/community field, not all online German rap. No mutually exclusive musical boundary is claimed. Positive creator-network/institutional practice, not a different arrangement, artist or viral view count alone, supports the narrower category.

extras.description: Rapped and sung phrases pass between performers over rhythmically grounded DJ accompaniment. Vocal exchanges, repeated hooks and a strong beat support direct lyrical delivery, while styles and production approaches vary across the wider scene.

tradition.name: Hip Hop Mauritanien
tradition.lineage: Mauritanian hip hop — a multilingual urban movement shaped by Senegalese and international rap from the 1990s, local production networks and the Assalamalekoum festival.

extras.description: Mauritanian hip hop developed through youth networks linking Nouakchott with Senegal and wider international rap. Rhythmic spoken delivery and produced beats carry social commentary, local identity and contemporary concerns across the country’s languages. Independent studios, discovery competitions and Assalamalekoum have helped connect performers, producers and audiences across regional communities.

entries.geo_rationale: Documented national production and festival hub, not sole musical origin.

Senegalese rap is an acknowledged foundational influence, while local production institutions, multilingual communities and national networks establish a distinct regional field. Maghreb’s older popular-music umbrella is not identical to this rap movement; no claim of unique physical instrumentation or sonic isolation.

Preserve two alternating rap participants; the challenger identity is not supplied. This is the specific complete challenge within the event, not the whole evening, its guest concerts or audience games. The organiser positively identifies the battle as acapella; no beat, DJ, instruments or sung chorus inferred. This is a documented announced practice, not a claim to have watched a complete recording or confirmed event execution. The organiser explicitly names Hong Kong Hip Hop and VEEHK, local WavySoundHK/SpecialPlan/M4-linked participants and Hong Kong/Macau performance circuits. This gives a local institutional rap field beyond nationality alone. Full Chinese Hip Hop already spans languages and regions, not only its Higher Brothers/Chengdu example; Hong Kong is an overlapping narrower city-community branch, not a disjoint invention of rap. Cantopop covers Cantonese popular song and can contain rap, but does not exhaust this specifically documented competitive hip-hop institution. Hong Kong Rock and TV Drama are different practice/function fields. No exact creator-map performer membership asserted: both direct map and1d retrieval failed, while organiser category evidence is explicit. All current and accepted queued regional rap scopes compared. mcRhythm.intlHipHop models the positive rap practice. Existing live-duet/live-ensemble controls represent the complete two-person pair across alternating rounds, not simultaneous harmony or a recorded choir. Physiological details and pitch organisation remain source-unspecified; rhythmic spoken articulation is supported by the stated rap battle. One voice card covers both participants, no extra musical audience inferred. Studio room and chain are an authored controlled rendition, not the outdoor carnival venue; global tuning omitted.

tradition.lineage: Úlfur Úlfur — complete Harpa Kaldalón Iceland Airwaves2015 set as witnessed by Columbia College Chicago correspondent Laura Kondourajian. The report names core rappers Arnar Freyr and Helgi Sæmundur, DJ Þorbjörn Einar, a live backing band with guitar, bass, organic drums, piano and electronic textures, and closing guest rapper Kött Grá Pjé. Retain all seven role families and three positively identified human vocal performers across the full set. Backing players and any doubling are not individually named; no total human headcount is invented. This is the report’s third complete act, not a combined AUÐUR/russian.girls/Úlfur programme or the different KEXP November7 set. Report heading dates day two November5 while one sentence says Wednesday; preserve that internal date discrepancy rather than manufacture a corrected exact day. No exact duration or complete song list claimed. Full seven-family authored concert rendition retains the two core MCs, closing guest and named DJ, all backing roles and unspecified electronic textures. Neutral credited-electronics owner preserves positive electronic sound without guessing synthesizer, sample, DAW or patch architecture; neutral DJ owner preserves actual DJ practice without assigning vinyl or decks. These roles may overlap in source production, but neither sound role is silently discarded. Generic piano is realized as a standard modern upright with block-chord articulation, explicitly authored rather than identified source subtype. Source-unspecified vocal physiology, pitch, ornament and speech/song balance remain neutral; group ensemble models the documented rap and melodic-pop practice including guest participation, not all three continuously simultaneous. Alder/maple/rosewood humbucker guitar, AlnicoII pickup, pure-nickel10-gauge strings, short scale, vibrato bridge and clean strum are authored. Alder soapbar bass with nickel roundwounds and locked fingerstyle, maple thin-shell kit/coated heads/45-degree edges/20 wires/single felt pedal/B20 traditional-finish fully lathed machine-hammered cymbals with rock sticks are coherent new physical realizations, not observed gear. Controlled live-room acoustics and brisk amplified concert energy are authored; no fixed measured BPM or original room acoustics are asserted. No global temperament or source amp is invented. International hip-hop parent describes the MC-led national scene without requiring newly invented harmony or drill production.

tradition.name: Korean Drill
tradition.lineage: Korean drill — South Korean rap adapting the rhythmic delivery and bass-heavy production of the international drill scene.

extras.description: Korean drill develops drill’s sparse, forceful beat language within South Korean hip-hop. Rapped verses ride deep electronic bass, programmed drums and economical melodic textures. Artists including Fleeky Bang draw on Bronx drill while developing local crews, language and performance styles. The sound participates in a shared drill lineage while belonging to Korea’s contemporary rap community.

entries.geo_rationale: Country-level editorial anchor for explicitly Korean localized rap practice; not a claimed qualifier venue.

Existing k_rap already includes contemporary production and Show Me the Money, and korean_hip_hop covers the broad national scene: neither is limited to old performers. Drill, UK Drill and Brooklyn Drill share lineage and can overlap this Korean adaptation; their broad diaspora does not make every national rap field equivalent. tradition.name: Lao Hip Hop
tradition.lineage: Lao hip hop connects rap and beat production in Laos with Lao diaspora communities, combining contemporary expression with local languages and cultural memory.

extras.description: Rhythmic verses and memorable hooks ride produced beats in Lao hip hop. Artists in Laos and the diaspora address everyday experience and identity in Lao and English, while some arrangements introduce the khaen mouth organ or draw on lam traditions. Concerts, cultural festivals and online collaborations link these varied approaches.

tradition.name: Magyar Trap
tradition.lineage: Magyar trap is Hungary’s contemporary trap scene, adapting 808-heavy hip-hop production to Hungarian-language verses, short hooks and playful ad-libs.

extras.description: Emerging artists including Lil Frakk, Lmen Prala and the AKC collective connect spacious rap phrasing with heavy electronic low end and programmed rhythm. Personal, ironic and confrontational lyrics coexist, while melodic delivery and pitch processing connect parts of the scene with pop. The local network developed through online releases, collaborations and energetic live audiences.

entries.geo_rationale: Editorial national-scene anchor at Budapest; the RTL report also documents Vác and a Budapest international concert, not a claim of exclusive birthplace.

sources.support_notes: Fresh direct turn13532view0. Firsthand Lil Frakk interview positively names Hungarian trap peers, contrasting spacious phrasing with older hip-hop and explicitly describing growling 808s, ad-libs and the local generational community.
Fresh direct turn13534view0. Broadcaster interviews Lmen Prala and AKC members; describes rap, short hooks, large bass, pitch processing and music-software production in the Hungarian trap scene.

tradition.name: Military Rap
tradition.lineage: Military rap is a hip-hop community shaped by service members and veterans, with songs addressing service, deployment, family and the return to civilian life. Recordings and performances connect artists with military and veteran audiences.

extras.description: Personal narrative and rhythmic spoken delivery lead the music, supported by rap production and recurring beats. Intimate unaccompanied versions also foreground the words; military subject matter does not require marching-band instrumentation or drill cadence.

entries.geo_rationale: Army primary identifies artist as from San Francisco; regional community anchor, not recording-session location.

It is not all rap made by somebody who served, a universal political viewpoint or a claim that every playlist member is a veteran. tradition.name: Persian Underground Hip Hop
tradition.lineage: Persian underground hip hop grew through independent Iranian and diaspora recording, circulation and performance networks, including the community around Hichkas and Moltafet.

extras.description: Forceful, conversational rap places Persian-language writing and social observation over rhythmic beat production. Independent releases and online circulation connect artists across Iran and the diaspora. The field overlaps broader Persian hip hop while emphasizing these independent creative networks.

entries.geo_rationale: The issued performance title explicitly names Melbourne. This is the selected performance anchor, not the birthplace or national extent of the Persian underground community.
entries.neighbor_distinction: Persian Underground Hip Hop is an overlapping independently circulated Iranian/Persian rap community, not merely all Persian-language rap or a claim that every listed artist remains commercially obscure. The exact creator map includes Hichkas, Bahram, Fadaei, Quf and other participants. In his firsthand2014 Index on Censorship interview Hichkas describes unauthorized physical circulation, alternative internet distribution, blocked domestic performances and diaspora-supported appearances; Moltafet own catalogue positively links the selected issuer and artist network. This supports a particular independent distribution and performance community within the broader Persian-language field. Full existing persian_hip_hop already includes Iran and diaspora and does not exclude underground artists; overlap is explicit, and its Bahman short freestyle is not treated as a definition limiting that umbrella. The proposed narrower institutional practice is not established by a different vocal edition alone. Persian electronic and Persian alternative describe other overlapping musical practices; naqqali is a narrative tradition rather than the contemporary MC distribution community. No membership or political position is inferred for every Persian rapper.

tradition.name: Pinoy Alternative Rap
tradition.lineage: Pinoy alternative rap develops through independent Philippine hip-hop communities that value artistic experimentation, collaboration and self-directed production. Networks such as UPRISING connect rappers and DJs across local languages and styles.

extras.description: Individual MC voices and contrasting flows interact with sampled beats, low bass and changing textures. Live performance, turntablism and collaborative production provide room for lyrical and sonic approaches outside a single mainstream formula.

entries.geo_rationale: Issuer identifies Tala and Supreme Fist in Quezon City, while Ilaya is Taguig; editorial network anchor, not claimed festival recording location.
entries.neighbor_distinction: Pinoy Alternative Rap is represented by a documented independent, artist-organized Philippine rap network rather than defined merely by do-it-yourself equipment or a noncommercial label. The festival issuer describes UPRISING as a self-produced grassroots network of emcees, turntablists and producers operating across Filipino, Bisaya and English, relying on its own artistic output rather than prevailing trends and industry machinery. Its shared festivals, tours, collaborative releases and online launches establish continuing community practice. The exact creator category includes named members Ilaya and Supreme Fist plus BLKD, UMPH, Illustrado, Emar Industriya, KJah and other members of this network. Kartel as a group name is absent from the inspected100-item creator sample; do not claim exact group or selected-song membership. Existing pinoy_hip_hop is a broad national/diasporic multilingual field and already embraces diverse live-band practices; Tagalog Rap already includes FlipTop and mass-market rap, and Pinoy Trap explicitly includes UPRISING among its historical collectives. These are acknowledged overlaps, not excluded populations. The proposed alternative discovery field is a narrower overlapping artist/community axis, not a claim every UPRISING recording is non-trap or that all independent rap sounds the same. Its source basis combines creator membership of actual performers with a positively self-organized alternative-to-industry network, not a different artist alone.

tradition.name: Polish Drill
tradition.lineage: Polish drill — Polish-language rap adapting British-influenced drill production and delivery.

extras.description: Polish drill brings Polish-language rap into the British-influenced drill sound, with forceful rhythmic verses over sparse melodies, electronic bass and sharply programmed drums. Artists such as Miszel connect local rap communities with international drill platforms. The field shares drill’s production vocabulary while developing its own language, performers and audience.

tradition.name: Polish underground rap
tradition.lineage: Polish underground rap developed through independent releases, DIY circulation and local club networks, including Warsaw’s experimental scene. Acts such as TONFA connect rap with turntablism, live percussion and cross-genre collaboration.

extras.description: Interacting rap voices work against scratched and cut recorded material and an energetic drum-kit pulse. Rhythmic speech, abrupt transitions and contrasting textures create a confrontational live sound within a wider field of independent production.

entries.geo_rationale: Warsaw is the independently documented home scene of TONFA and named collaborators; selected event occurs in London, explicitly retained separately.

tradition.lineage: Kamba pop connects vernacular song in eastern Kenya with benga bands, recordings and contemporary dance audiences. Artists such as Ken Wa Maria and Kativui Mweene carry narrative and topical lyrics through a guitar-driven popular tradition that includes both secular and gospel repertoires.

extras.description: Lead and supporting singing interlock with bright electric-guitar figures, an active bass line and a steady drum pulse. Repeated refrains and instrumental passages create room for dancing, with contrasting accents and melodic guitar responses keeping the texture in motion.

extras.description: Sung melodies meet amplified guitar, bass and drums, with some fusion groups bringing bamboo flute, reed instruments and Karbi drums into the band. Arak exemplifies this interplay of local instrumental colors and energetic popular-song arrangement.

entries.geo_rationale: Country-only editorial anchor for explicitly Karbi Anglong/Dima Hasao community practice; not a measured recording site or a claim all India is Karbi-speaking.
entries.neighbor_distinction: Karbi Pop denotes the contemporary Karbi-language popular recording and performance community within Assam, with folk-derived and modern song forms. The exact creator playlist contains contemporary song artists, Warklung and Dhansing Teron, and is not exclusively electronic commercial pop. Arak is not found in that retrieved92-item sample, so exact band membership is not asserted. The band’s firsthand account positively describes a regional song/video/film industry and cultural awards, youth-facing modern treatment of Karbi melodies and its own place in that circulation. This supplies an independent community bridge rather than birthplace alone. Existing Assamese Pop is the Assamese-language popular field, overlapping but not equivalent to the Karbi-language community; Indian Indie and Northeast regional scenes are broader or differently situated. No claim excludes cross-language or folk-revival participation. Contemporary arrangement is the selected branch, not a universal Karbi-pop palette or a claim that traditional songs become unrelated new genres.

tradition.name: Karen Pop
tradition.lineage: Karen pop connects contemporary popular music with Karen communities in Myanmar and the diaspora. Artists draw on personal experience, migration and multilingual expression while working across pop and related modern styles.

extras.description: Melodic singing can sit over a bass-and-drum foundation with synthesizer, piano and string textures. Softer songs favour connected vocal lines and rounded accompaniment, while other releases draw on more forceful electronic or hip-hop production.

entries.geo_rationale: Artist first-person diaspora home/practice San Diego, not genre-exclusive origin or original recording room.
entries.neighbor_distinction: Karen Pop is the Karen popular-music and diaspora community field rather than all Myanmar national pop. Firsthand Star2 interview explicitly connects his music upbringing, bilingual English/Karen rap and ongoing work to Karen community music; the creator KarenPop playlist freshly includes Star2 with ChinaTownRunner at item31 and multilingual regional/diaspora performers. The selected English-language reggae-pop love song illustrates one documented mapped participant’s popular practice, not a claim every Karen song is reggae or exclusively Karen-language. Queued myanmar_gospel instead specifies Burmese-language Christian praise, not this secular diasporic popular field. tradition.name: Kumaoni Pop
tradition.lineage: Kumaoni pop — Kumaon’s regional-language popular songs, bringing local melodies and folk rhythms into contemporary recorded arrangements.

extras.description: Kumaoni pop adapts the Kumaoni language and regional song heritage to contemporary listening and dance settings. Folk-derived melodies and hudka rhythms meet guitar, keyboard or piano accompaniment and modern recording production. Artists connect village traditions, family occasions and regional identity with younger audiences and online circulation.

entries.geo_rationale: Kumaon regional editorial anchor, not source recording address.

sources.title: First-person Pandavaas production interview
sources.support_notes: Fresh indexed13468search0 full interview, retained unmodified raw response. Explicit regional folk modernization, Kumaoni-language work, and hudka/piano/guitar combination. Direct page bot challenge disclosed.

sources.title: Indian Music Experience Museum: Hudak
sources.support_notes: Fresh13468view0 documents wooden hourglass, two goat-hide heads, underarm hold and pitch control from connecting strings.

entries.neighbor_distinction: Kumaoni Pop is the Kumaon/Kumaoni-language community within the broader Pahadi popular-music field. It overlaps neighboring Garhwali Pop and Himachali Pop through musicians and instrumentation but has a distinct regional-language repertoire; Pandavaas works across regional languages and is not exclusively Kumaoni. Existing broad Indian Pop does not exhaust this local field. No new physical sound is claimed simply from a language distinction.
entries.model_policy: Genre-level representative folk-pop arrangement informed by practitioner discussion of combining hudka with piano, guitar and singing. Not a reconstruction of one master or exact performer count. A single accompanied singer, strummed small-body parlor guitar with silk-and-steel strings, block-chord upright piano and hand-struck pressure drum are authored choices. All positive source families retained; unspecified recording models are not facts. tradition.name: Ladakhi pop
tradition.lineage: Ladakhi pop carries Ladakhi-language song into contemporary recordings, media and live performance. Regional song traditions and neighbouring Himalayan influences meet modern popular arrangements, while intimate acoustic performances sustain the connection between melody, poetry and everyday life.

extras.description: Expressive singing is supported by guitar in acoustic settings and by fuller arrangements in recorded pop. Love songs and regional identity remain important threads across these approaches.
exemplars: Rigzin Norbu — Lungspo ju ju, firsthand documented acoustic rendition

entries.neighbor_distinction: Ladakhi-language popular song has a documented regional media and practitioner history, with rural heritage and neighbouring Himalayan influences. It overlaps Himalayan folk, Tibetan pop and Nepali pop without being coextensive: the full existing Himalayan folk covers village repertories across the mid-Himalayan belt; Nepali pop is a Kathmandu-centred Nepali-language industry; Tibetan pop remains a broad Tibetan popular field, not merely its current experimental exemplar. This selected intimate acoustic love-song cover supports balladPoetry, not a claim that all Ladakhi pop has two sound families.

tradition.lineage: Lao pop brings contemporary popular-song writing into dialogue with Lao musical heritage and regional Asian pop exchange.

tradition.name: Maluku Pop
tradition.lineage: Maluku pop grew through Moluccan bands, recordings and diaspora networks linking eastern Indonesia with the Netherlands. Indorock, soul, fusion and contemporary dance music meet regional melodies and multilingual songwriting, with artists such as Massada, Daniel Sahuleka and the Moluccan Moods Orchestra contributing different strands.

extras.description: Lead and harmony singing ride a guitar, bass and drum foundation, with keyboards, auxiliary percussion and lyrical wind lines adding color. Memorable refrains alternate with instrumental passages and improvisatory responses, drawing regional song traditions into contemporary popular arrangements.

entries.geo_rationale: Venue locality for selected diaspora programme, not origin of all Maluku music or performer birthplace.
entries.neighbor_distinction: Maluku Pop is the contemporary Moluccan popular-music community, including its Dutch diaspora circulation and cross-style original pop, rap and dance releases. Primary participant research by Rein Spoorman documents Moluccan pop networks and Moluccan Moods programmes across styles, not only inherited regional songs; the venue documents a current recurring Moluccan community event. Exact creator corpus contains contemporary Dutch-language releases and regional-song remixes. Accepted Lagu Maluku defines the broader regional song-repertoire axis and is not restricted to its selected classical piano rhapsody or to old songs. Considerable overlap remains; this proposed modern popular-community axis includes original international/Dutch-language pop beyond adaptation of inherited Maluku tunes. Existing Lagu Timur expressly covers Maluku within broader Eastern Indonesian song circulation; Indonesian Pop and Dutch Pop are broader national fields, not restricted to selected exemplars. Category distinction rests on independently documented community/circulation and the exact creator corpus, not a different DJ or country alone; no mutually exclusive boundary is claimed.

tradition.name: Oromo Pop
tradition.lineage: Documented contemporary Jimma Oromo electric popular-band practice of Shenen Gibe Band, described firsthand by recording issuer Sheba Sound in January2015. The group regularly practices in the town cinema with electric keyboard, bass guitar, lead guitar and western drum kit; the issuer positively identifies its whole morning electric session, distinct from the separate afternoon traditional Hagerigna session. Six named vocalists plus Weynishet Shimelis dance/vocals are retained across the practice, without assuming every singer performs every song simultaneously. No dance footstep percussion is invented. This models the complete documented band practice, not a claim that a selected individual track contains the entire roster. Afternoon krar/kebero, separate Manasseh dub and general cultural-office masinqo discussion are not morning-band credits. An authored contemporary Oromo popular-band rendition keeps all five positive role families. Seven credited singers across the practice are represented with a combined live group and live ensemble stack, not a claim of simultaneous original harmonies or absence of overdubs. Connected syllabic singing is an authored choice consistent with positively sung love songs, with neutral unknown physiology and lineage. Source lead guitar is authored clean-strummed alder/maple single-coil electric, bass dual-single electric with roundwound strings, and western kit maple/coated-head stick backbeat; exact source models, woods, skins and notes are not claimed. Bare keyboard retains unspecified electronic architecture. An authored functional-harmonic verse-chorus-bridge popular-song arrangement is deliberate, not a transcription of original Oromo harmony or form. A treated concert-hall listening rendition is authored for the positively documented theatre-stage practice. Broad natural room response supports a shared band and vocal-group space; shoebox geometry, decay and stereo capture are editorial choices, not measured Jimma venue facts. No global tuning or capture apparatus asserted.

Existing himachali_pop already represents the broad Himachali contemporary popular/discovery field, not only Moksh rock or metal; it overlaps substantially and also includes the selected artist. The proposed distinction is the broader cross-regional usage of Pahadi Pop, not different instrumentation, date or an exclusion of Rathi from Himachali Pop. Existing Garhwali/Kumaoni regional popular categories can likewise overlap. Creator roster concentration is acknowledged: current Pahadi playlist leans strongly Himachali and alone does not prove a disjoint sound or exclusive geographic boundary. No equivalence or universal single language is asserted.

tradition.name: Palestinian Pop
tradition.lineage: Palestinian pop encompasses contemporary popular music shaped by Palestinian communities and their wider regional and diasporic connections. Singers and groups bring Arabic song, inherited melodies, dance rhythms, hip-hop and electronic production into a varied popular repertoire.

extras.description: Melodic vocals and rhythmic accompaniment span intimate songs, modern band arrangements and electronic dance music. The live-percussion and synthesizer interplay of Shamstep is one prominent branch of this wider field.

tradition.name: PNG pop
tradition.lineage: PNG pop is Papua New Guinea’s contemporary popular-song field, joining local melodies and languages with rock, reggae, country-pop, R&B and other international styles.

extras.description: Catchy singing and rhythmic accompaniment connect diverse local communities through recordings, radio and live performance. Electric guitar, bass, drums and keyboards support one widely used band setting, while string bands and electronic productions offer other textures. Island-reggae grooves, pop melody and regional musical traditions circulate together without reducing the country’s many styles to a single sound.

entries.geo_rationale: Editorial national popular-music hub; not exclusive origin or selected performance venue.

sources.support_notes: Fresh13572view0 original label explicitly documents national popular-performance practice spanning country-pop, traditional, reggae, hip-hop and jazz, with bass,guitar,drums,two keyboards and four featured artists. Supports representative band roles, not a reconstructed live recording.

Fresh13572view1 firsthand interview describes PNG independent/radio scene and his island-pop mixture of reggae,zouk,dancehall,reggaeton and R&B; melody-centered songwriting. Supports national pop field, not a fixed all-genre instrument inventory.

tradition.name: Polish Viral Pop
tradition.lineage: Polish viral pop developed through online creators, video channels and fan communities that grew into recording and concert networks. Projects such as EKIPA and Genzie connect pop hooks, rap, trap and R&B with personal stories, collective identities and rapidly shared audiovisual releases.

extras.description: Sung hooks, rapped passages and overlapping vocal personalities sit above producer-shaped accompaniment. Repeated motifs, direct refrains and contrasts between reflective and party-oriented sections keep the vocal message at the center of a broad contemporary pop sound.

entries.geo_rationale: National language/creator community anchor explicitly supported by creator field and publisher Polish-pop classification; not a guessed original recording town.

It does not imply every creator-playlist artist is an influencer or that mainstream singers cannot cross into the field. entries.neighbor_distinction: Pop Flamenco is the positively named popular-song crossover and circulation field, with substantial overlap with Nuevo Flamenco, traditional flamenco artists and Spanish pop. It is not defined by a supposedly disjoint artist list or by this duo instrumentation. A contemporaneous1994 Music and Media firsthand interview with Compadres publisher Adrian Vogel explicitly distinguishes pop-flamenco popular-audience arrangements/production from the broader tradition-led Nuevo Flamenco innovation; Nuevos Medios founder Mario Pacheco discusses the overlapping movement, and the article itself identifies Rosario material crossing both. This is a documented practical distinction, not a timeless purity boundary or a claim Nuevo Flamenco excludes pop. The current duo expressly uses pop-flamenco for its acoustic popular repertoire, and the exact creator category includes its named repertoire artists Niña Pastori, Antonio Orozco, India Martínez, Vanesa Martín and Estopa. The duo itself is not claimed to appear in the creator sample. Full old nuevo_flamenco already includes pop production/jazz/Latin fusion; old flamenco itself distinguishes later pop/fusion from cante-foreground traditional practice. Spanish popular-song fields remain overlapping broader contexts. The new entry represents the explicitly named popular-song branch rather than rewriting the broader old fusion field or defining it as strictly noncommercial.

tradition.name: Pop Flamenco
tradition.lineage: Julia Gaz and Claudia de la Torre — whole current artist-described acoustic duo practice, voice and piano. Their first-person booking profile explicitly defines the complete two-person formation, more than40 Spanish-language hits, and a flexible performance of up to two hours. Julia sings and Claudia plays piano; one singer, one pianist. This selects the whole offered duo configuration, not an invented extraction from a larger produced master or a claim that an individual booking occurred. The repertoire spans pop-flamenco and Spanish pop from ballads to danceable material; all of that mixed programme remains included. Exact piano architecture, vocal register, score voicings, source tempo and realized setlist remain unknown. Broad functionalSong/pop is an explicitly authored verse-chorus-bridge popular-song rendition over functional harmonic progressions, not a transcription of every original song or source arrangement. One accompanied singer retains unspecified physiology/register/ornament and a natural unprocessed voice; no cante-jondo technique or twelve-beat compás is inferred from the category label. Source-unspecified piano is authored as a standard studio upright with connected legato and pedal resonance in a controlled live room, not measured source equipment. Brisk vocal pacing, where rendered, is an intentionally energetic presentation of the source-described danceable branch, not the original tempo of all ballads. No global tuning or capture apparatus is inferred.

Pop Flamenco is the positively named popular-song crossover and circulation field, with substantial overlap with Nuevo Flamenco, traditional flamenco artists and Spanish pop. It is not defined by a supposedly disjoint artist list or by this duo instrumentation. A contemporaneous1994 Music and Media firsthand interview with Compadres publisher Adrian Vogel explicitly distinguishes pop-flamenco popular-audience arrangements/production from the broader tradition-led Nuevo Flamenco innovation; Nuevos Medios founder Mario Pacheco discusses the overlapping movement, and the article itself identifies Rosario material crossing both. This is a documented practical distinction, not a timeless purity boundary or a claim Nuevo Flamenco excludes pop. The current duo expressly uses pop-flamenco for its acoustic popular repertoire, and the exact creator category includes its named repertoire artists Niña Pastori, Antonio Orozco, India Martínez, Vanesa Martín and Estopa. The duo itself is not claimed to appear in the creator sample. Spanish popular-song fields remain overlapping broader contexts. The new entry represents the explicitly named popular-song branch rather than rewriting the broader old fusion field or defining it as strictly noncommercial. Source-unspecified piano is authored as a standard studio upright with connected legato and pedal resonance in a controlled live room, not measured source equipment. Brisk vocal pacing, where rendered, is an intentionally energetic presentation of the source-described danceable branch, not the original tempo of all ballads. tradition.name: Pop Urbaine
tradition.lineage: Pop urbaine is a contested Francophone broadcasting and industry label for crossings between melodic pop and hip-hop.

extras.description: Prominent sung hooks, rhythmic vocal phrasing and beat-led accompaniment connect rap, R&B and dance-oriented pop. Artists such as Aya Nakamura and Bramsito illustrate this broad crossover; the label describes musical circulation rather than ethnicity.

entries.geo_rationale: Country-only editorial anchor for the positively documented French broadcasting/industry field. Not a recording site, artist birthplace or exclusion of Belgian/diasporic Francophone participation.
entries.neighbor_distinction: Pop Urbaine is treated as a contested Francophone crossover industry and broadcasting field, not an ethnicity or a universally accepted artist identity. Generations firsthand interviews document both a practitioner account of melodic hip-hop/pop crossover and a manager rejecting the label as reductive; Skyrock itself uses the term for its Aya Nakamura programming, and CNM original industry research describes this named danceable Francophone hip-hop-influenced export field. The exact creator playlist includes rap-heavy material and Bramsito/Booba, so the category is not defined as exclusively singing or as an exclusive artist roster. Aya was not found in the retrieved100-item creator sample; her bridge is direct broadcaster usage, not claimed creator membership. Full existing French Rap already includes contemporary cloud/trap, and Rap Francais the researched contemporary metadata branch; neither is being restricted to old or nonmelodic rap. The additional axis is the positively documented pop-crossover broadcasting/industry field spanning rap and sung pop, with substantial overlap. French Pop and Classic French Pop are broader popular-song fields whose chosen guitar or retrospective examples do not exclude this repertoire. Urban Contemporary is a distinct US radio-format institution, not a French translation of this contested Francophone field. Nouvelle Vague describes another overlapping producer/rap branch. No difference is inferred merely from choosing a solo piano arrangement, skin colour or performer nationality.

tradition.name: Sambalpuri Pop
tradition.lineage: Sambalpuri pop connects the western Odisha regional-language recording scene with older broadcast hits and contemporary popular releases.

extras.description: Regional vocal melodies can be recast with electric guitar, bass, drums and keyboards. Shared singing and occasional rap expand the contemporary band sound, while repertoire such as Rangabati links new arrangements to the region’s recorded-song heritage.

entries.geo_rationale: Editorial regional-repertoire anchor explicitly named by issuer and AIR Sambalpur; original mixing/mastering took place in Mumbai, not a claimed Sambalpur session.
entries.neighbor_distinction: Sambalpuri Pop is the western-Odisha Sambalpuri-language popular recording field, with both older recorded folk hits and contemporary digital song releases. Exact creator100-track roster positively includes the original Rangabati by Jitendriya Haripal and Krishna Patel at35 and61 alongside newer regional artists. The verified adaptation issuer explicitly identifies that original recording and its Sambalpur origin, closing the repertoire bridge without claiming the remake artists themselves occur in the current creator roster. Existing odia_pop already spans Odisha broadcasting, films, cassette albums and contemporary videos; Sambalpuri is an overlapping narrower regional-language community, not a claim the broader Odia field excludes it. The narrower regional institutional presence is independently documented by All India Radio Sambalpur maintaining an expressly Sambalpuri music artist category. Existing desi_pop describes the broader national non-film market, and odia_bhajan the specifically devotional-purpose field; neither is synonymous with this regional popular-song field. The chosen mixed-language contemporary arrangement is one branch, not evidence all Sambalpuri pop uses Tamil rap or this instrumentation.

tradition.name: Santali Pop
tradition.lineage: Santali pop — contemporary popular songs in the Santal language, carried by cassette and video production, regional performers and a newer generation of online musicians.

extras.description: Santali pop brings Santal-language melodies, romance and community concerns into contemporary popular-song formats. Cassette and video industries helped build regional audiences, while online performers now revisit earlier songs and make new acoustic and electronically produced recordings. Traditional musical memory, neighboring popular styles and youthful experimentation coexist across this varied field.

entries.neighbor_distinction: Santali Pop is a language/community popular-music field across eastern India, not an alias for Bengali Baul. The actual Baul row describes a Bengali mystic-itinerant tradition and its specific lineage; modern Santali music can borrow from Baul but also includes love songs, commercial videos and contemporary covers. West Bengali Pop describes a neighboring state/language popular field and does not cover the broader Santali-language community across Jharkhand, Odisha and adjacent regions. Acoustic treatment here is representative, not a claim that all Santali pop is acoustic or separate from Indian popular music.
entries.model_policy: Representative acoustic pop rendition within the documented modern Santali field, informed by the Soren cousins’ firsthand account of singing with guitar, ukulele and cajón. All positively described families are retained; no claim of reconstructing one video, simultaneous original instruments, five original singers or exact band personnel. A single accompanied sung lead, compact silk-and-steel parlor guitar, mahogany concert ukulele and ordinary unsnared rear-port cajón are explicit authored choices where source construction is unspecified. Neutral cajón role avoids importing festejo/marinera repertoire. Functional-harmonic verse-chorus-bridge arrangement, syllabic delivery and spacious acoustic-recital capture are authored popular-song choices, not measured source settings.
entries.source_scope_limitation: Genre-level practice synthesis. Source singer count and exact simultaneous tracking unknown; chosen lead and acoustic construction are authored. Traditional madol/flute and electronic variants remain part of the wider field, not falsely declared absent.

tradition.name: Sorani Pop
tradition.lineage: Sorani pop centres on contemporary song in the Sorani Kurdish language, circulated through recordings, television and concert performance. Traditional melodies and poetry remain influential as singers and composers develop modern arrangements and collaborate across Kurdish and neighbouring musical traditions.

extras.description: Melodic singing leads arrangements ranging from compact popular accompaniment to concert ensembles with plucked and bowed strings, santur, hand percussion and piano. Regional vocal expression connects inherited repertoire with contemporary songwriting.
exemplars: Adnan Karim and Hezaravaz Ensemble — complete announced16May2025 concert ensemble

entries.neighbor_distinction: Exact creator Sorani Pop corpus names Adnan Karim36 and Bokan Hawrami41 within a contemporary Sorani-language recording/discovery community. Bullock’s firsthand research documents this Sorani/Hewrami television-song circulation and its traditional-song genealogy; selected artist is also explicitly Kurdish/Persian concert practice in the venue primary. Existing kurdish_pop is a broad cross-language contemporary Kurdish umbrella and includes overlapping artists; this narrower named linguistic/media repertoire does not exclude it. Kurdish folk likewise includes overlapping inherited melodies, while dengbej specifically preserves bardic recital rather than the whole contemporary recorded-song field. Kurdish rock and hiphop are distinct style branches that may also overlap the creator corpus. No category boundary rests on this eight-role example alone, nor on treating Kurdish Pop as limited to its Rewsan example. Existing Turkish makam and Persian modal traditions describe modal practice systems rather than this named Sorani discovery community.

tradition.lineage: Independent power-pop communities linked by small labels, fanzines, mail-order distribution and festivals, including the International Pop Overthrow network.

extras.description: Melodic guitar songs combine bright chordal hooks, lead and harmony vocals, electric bass and a firm drum backbeat. Keyboards can add colour to the compact band sound. The underground field connects independent artists and listeners across countries through specialist labels, publications and shared bills, continuing the wider power-pop tradition.

tradition.name: 8D
tradition.lineage: 8D audio is an online headphone-listening practice that makes recorded music appear to move around the listener through binaural spatial processing. It circulates across pop, rap, electronic and other repertoires rather than prescribing a particular band or compositional style.

extras.description: 8D versions use spatial processing to create a moving, surrounding impression over headphones. A stereo song mix can be treated as a single moving source, while more elaborate productions position separate instruments in virtual space. HRTF filtering and reflected sound help convey external location beyond ordinary left-right volume panning.

sources.support_notes: Fresh turn13437view0 manufacturer explicitly defines typical8D as binaural rendering of whole stereo mixdown, with object-positioning as advanced alternative.
Fresh turn13437view1 manufacturer documents HRTF, azimuth/elevation, width, reflection level/length/material and Focus externalization control; automatable movement.
Producer-library publisher explains rotating headphone listening and spatial treatment.

entries.model_policy: Representative whole-mix binaural-rendering workflow positively documented by manufacturer. Non-individualized HRTF, ear-level orbit, moderate short reflections and balanced focus are authored spatial choices, not measurements of an identified remix. This data record describes a rendering process; it does not implement an audio DSP engine. No health claim, eight physical dimensions, source BPM or global temperament asserted.
entries.neighbor_distinction: Existing binaural record concerns paired-frequency binaural-beat listening with Mellotron; this field instead spatializes arbitrary musical programmes. Ambient and electronic fields overlap repertoire but do not define this headphone motion-processing practice. Dummy-head microphone capture and simple stereo auto-pan are different mechanisms and are not substituted for HRTF rendering.

tradition.name: Cantaditas
tradition.lineage: Cantaditas is a Spanish dance-music repertoire centered on memorable sung hooks and familiar club anthems. Remember parties and festivals carry late-1990s and early-2000s recordings into contemporary DJ culture, linking vocal dance songs across related electronic styles.

extras.description: Foreground vocal refrains and repeating dance rhythms give the songs their immediate appeal. DJs connect familiar melodies and energetic recorded arrangements into continuous sets, with repetition and transitions sustaining the shared dance-floor momentum.

tradition.name: Cartoni Animati
tradition.lineage: Italian cartoon-theme music developed through television commissions, theme-song singles and collections such as Fivelandia. The songs connect generations of viewers with performers including Cristina D’Avena and Giorgio Vanni, while festival bands reshape familiar melodies through pop, rock and dance arrangements.

extras.description: Clear lead singing and supporting voices project recognizable melodies over electric guitar, bass, drums and keyboards. Short instrumental hooks, emphatic refrains and contrasting verse sections favor direct audience participation and an energetic pop-rock sound.

Exact creator corpus contains Giorgio Vanni Dragon Ball, Katia Svizzero L’Ape Maia and Elisabetta Viviani Heidi, bridging this institutional repertoire to the source label. This narrower Italian broadcasting, record-series and fan-event network overlaps Cartoon, anime themes and Italian pop, rather than being a synonym of all animation music or distinguished by a new pianist. Selected mixed anthology includes wider repertoire and is one documented Italian-market adaptation branch, not a definition that all32 works arose in that network.

tradition.name: Classic bhangra
tradition.lineage: Classic bhangra revisits the Punjabi bands and repertoire that shaped British Asian dance music during the late twentieth century. Groups such as Anjaana and Achanak link Punjabi folk singing and percussion with the development of UK bhangra, alongside the continuing influence of singers such as Kuldeep Manak.

extras.description: Strong dhol rhythms support Punjabi singing, with harmonium and hand drums sustaining the folk-band strand of the repertoire. Larger band arrangements and electronic production also belong to its history and later performance life.
exemplars: Anjaana — separately offered four-piece pure Panjabi folk practice

tradition.name: Cumbia Cristiana
tradition.lineage: Cumbia cristiana brings Christian lyrics and devotional themes into cumbia’s dance-song traditions. Bands and singers connect congregational and family audiences with the rhythmic vocabulary of contemporary Latin American popular music.

extras.description: Sung verses and recurring refrains ride a repeating bass line and interlocking percussion. Keyboards supply melody and chordal accompaniment, while güiro scraping and timbales accents sustain the dance pulse. Accordion, piano and electronic percussion add further colours in some bands.
exemplars: Lucho Dee Jay — complete Mix Remix CRISTIANOS / Cumbia WORSHIP programme, May 24, 2024

tradition.name: Cumbia Ecuatoriana
tradition.lineage: Ecuadorian cumbia adapts the wider Colombian-derived dance tradition through local orchestras, singers and later electronic production. Don Medardo y sus Players is a major reference within this national tropical-music community.

extras.description: Voices and melodic horn lines meet electric bass, keyboards and interlocking percussion. Repeated dance patterns support memorable refrains, with live-orchestra textures and synthesized arrangements both contributing to the evolving sound.

entries.geo_rationale: Municipal museum institutional repertoire-community anchor in Loja, where its2015 own tribute documents Don Medardo and national cumbia. Not DJ birthplace or selected mix recording location.
entries.neighbor_distinction: The DJ positively names cumbia ecuatoriana as one of the complete selected programme repertoires and separately issues an Ecuadorian-cumbia-tagged tribute to Don Medardo. Loja municipal museum own2015 tribute independently identifies the orchestra with a distinctive national cumbia practice and international circulation. That establishes community/repertoire evidence beyond a performers birthplace. The creator corpus was recovered separately and includes Juanita Burbano, Hipatia Balseca, Jaime Enrique Aymara, Gerardo Moran and Trio Colonial; it overlaps broader Ecuadorian popular music. Neither DJ TiaN nor the exact DeTodoMix is claimed as a named creator-playlist member, and no unretrieved tracklist is used to assert a matching song. Existing tecnocumbia explicitly includes both Peru and Ecuador and its1990s synth/programmed successor practice; national cumbia encompasses that development and earlier live-orchestra community, so the two overlap without being lexical equivalents. Existing cumbia_colombiana includes its original coastal practice and continental orchestral diaspora; Ecuadorian adaptation remains related rather than falsely independent of it. Peruvian/chicha and Bolivian records describe their own migration/regional-production histories, not all Andean cumbia. Ecuadorian Pop is a broader national popular-song field, not exclusively Juan Fernando Velasco or romantic songs. The full selected cross-style DJ programme is one contemporary circulation practice, not a definition that all Ecuadorian cumbia is DJ-produced or electronic.

tradition.name: Cumbia Santafesina
tradition.lineage: Cumbia Santafesina developed through Santa Fe’s dance bands, establishing local guitar-led and accordion-led strands within Argentina’s cumbia history. Los del Bohío and later regional groups helped shape a recognizable provincial scene.

extras.description: Sung melodies ride a steady bass foundation and interlocking percussion, with electric guitar or accordion carrying the melodic identity. Timbales, congas and electronic multipads can combine in contemporary live bands.

entries.geo_rationale: Source identifies Santa Fe band/community; approximate city anchor, not Córdoba interview-studio or a measured live performance location.
entries.neighbor_distinction: Cumbia Santafesina is the documented Santa Fe cumbia community and guitar/accordion lineages, not simply any band born in Santa Fe. Firsthand radio identifies this group and practice within that named field; Argentine interpreters association AADI separately documents Juan Carlos Denis/Los del Bohío guitar-led historical development away from the earlier Colombian accordion model. The earlier municipal Grupo Cali source confirms the parallel accordion-led practice; it is not omitted from a purported universal genre definition. Full cumbia_colombiana includes original Caribbean roots and international commercial spread; the Santa Fe field overlaps that ancestry but has a positively documented local historical network. Full cumbia_pop crosses Argentina/Uruguay/Mexico as a radio-facing hybrid, not all Santafesina history. Cumbia electrónica is sample/remix-production practice; a live Octapad does not automatically make this the same field. Cumbia villera, Peruvian, Uruguayan and Mexican regional traditions overlap repertoire/instruments without making their whole scope Santa Fe. Not a claim that guitars alone distinguish categories or all bands use this source palette.

tradition.lineage: Los Girasoles — complete current five-person stage practice described firsthand by leader Carlos Núñez in the30September2026 Radio La Ranchada interview: himself guitar/voice, Octapad player, timbales player, congas player and bassist. One positively named singer, five people and six instrument-family cards because voice/guitar doubles. This is the whole explicitly enumerated stage ensemble, not assumed instrumentation of the separately mentioned A mi querida madre single or an arbitrary reduced old Grupo Cali roster. No duration, tracklist, individual backing-member names, exact Octapad model or audio audition claimed. The interview explicitly contrasts the real band practice with soloists over backing tracks; no backing-master or invented guest imported. Broad functionalSong is an explicitly authored functional-harmonic verse–chorus–bridge song realization, not a measured claim about every source performance. Generic source guitar and bass receive candid modern electric realizations: clean-strummed alder humbucker guitar/maple neck/rosewood board/pure nickel strings and alder long-scale fretted soapbar bass/fingerstyle roundwounds; source exact electrical architecture/materials unknown. Shared alder body is coherent on both, all owning controls retained. Timbales retain stick-played steel-shell model with an authored foundational paila pattern, not an assertion of actual Cuban-son repertoire. Congas retain hands-layered middle-register Siam-oak/cowhide realization; middle role is an editorial representative register, not proof source had only one drum. Source-unspecified voice physiology stays neutral; single accompanied live lead and current-stage/no-overdub rendition are editorial realization of the documented one-singer live band, not studio single tracking. New Octapad identity preserves the positive multipad electronic trigger role while actual model/internal-or-external generator/presets/routing remain unknown. Manufacturer establishes8-pad Octapad architecture across PAD8/SPD30 history; no rubber, MIDI-only or internal-sampler sound assumed. Authored stick strikes and live dynamics are credible playing choices, not measured source strokes. Controlled live room is editorial; no historic gear/capture/tuning claims.

tradition.name: Experimental Big Band
tradition.lineage: Experimental Big Band extends large-ensemble jazz through collective improvisation, unconventional orchestration and the meeting of composed structures with open forms. Free-jazz orchestras and later creative big bands offer different approaches within this field.

extras.description: Contrasting reed registers, low winds and rhythm-section textures can build dense collective passages or open into sparse exchanges. Sectional writing and individual improvisation interact, with some ensembles also drawing on rock or minimalism.

tradition.lineage: Focus brings together music selected for concentration, including contemporary piano, ambient textures and instrumental beats. Streaming-era listening collections connect these different musical practices through a shared use during study and other sustained tasks.

tradition.name: Folklore Peruano
tradition.lineage: Folklore Peruano encompasses Peru’s diverse regional folk-song and dance traditions, including highland and coastal repertoires. Community performance, regional instruments and recorded folk repertoires sustain this broad national field.

extras.description: Vocal melody and patterned accompaniment take different forms across regions. Solo singing with a resonant Peruvian harp offers one intimate highland setting; larger instrumental and dance ensembles provide other textures.

entries.neighbor_distinction: Folklore Peruano is the national folk-repertoire discovery field, positively encompassing coastal and highland practices rather than a single huayno rhythm or one Andean instrument. Exact creator corpus spans regional performers including the selected Smithsonian artist. Peruvian congressional cultural analysis explicitly includes coastal marinera/tondero alongside highland traditions in the national folkloric field. Existing huayno_peruano and andean_huayno cover huayno across their full regional variants; they are not restricted to a particular harp/violin example. Música Andina is a pan-Andean repertoire field spanning countries, while this national field includes Peru’s coastal practices as well. Música Criolla Perú and Música Afroperuana cover specific coastal traditions; their substantial overlap is acknowledged. Música Ayacuchana is geographically narrower than this nationwide field. National coverage is independently supported, not inferred solely from the selected Cusco track or translation of an existing label.
entries.model_policy: Broad balladPoetry is a candid authored text-forward solo song rendition with sparse self-accompanied harp, not a claim of translated narrative, fixed score form or Mande griot lineage. Neutral source-unspecified voice physiology/register/pitch/ornament controls retained; syllabic singing and single unprocessed lead are authored presentation choices, actual tracking unknown. Peruvian harp is a genuinely absent physical identity: source-backed triangular frame/large resonance box, regional variable stringing and diatonic layout. The selected1962 instrument’s exact dimensions, string count/material allocation, wood and pitch standard are unknown. Cedar resonance wood is an explicit representative construction choice documented by Ferrier, not measured Ayala equipment. Both-hand bass/treble finger plucking follows performer-pedagogue practice, not a claimed exact transcription. String-count/material configuration remains source-unspecified; no forced Paraguayan/Jarocho identity, pedal/lever mechanism, glissandi or foreign repertoire. Controlled live room, neutral axes and optional apparatus omission are authored capture scaffolding; global temperament omitted. Brisk text-forward pacing and consoling harp affect are authored rendition choices, not measured original tempo, fixed ceremonial mood or translated lyric meaning.

tradition.name: Frafra
tradition.lineage: Frafra music belongs to the Frafra-speaking communities of northern Ghana, especially the Upper East region. Local song traditions continue through regional performers and contemporary recording networks connecting acoustic practice with amplified popular music.

extras.description: Text-forward singing can be accompanied by the struck and tossed calabash rattle called sinyaka, while other settings use kologo and fuller ensembles. Rhythmic vocal phrasing and recurring instrumental patterns give intimate performances a strong forward motion.

tradition.name: Gumbé
tradition.lineage: Gumbé is a diverse Guinea-Bissau popular-music field that draws local traditions into modern band performance and Lusophone musical exchange.

extras.description: Lead and supporting voices move over interlocking guitar, bass, drums and percussion, with keyboard harmony adding colour. Rhythmic dance-song arrangements connect the ensemble, while different local influences produce varied grooves and textures.

entries.geo_rationale: Producer locates assembled diaspora project and rehearsing/recording in Lisbon. Community project anchor, not Guinea-Bissau origin claim or exact performance venue.
entries.neighbor_distinction: Producer Francisco Fininho Sousa's first-person account explicitly names modern Gumbé as a diverse Bissau musical field drawing several local traditions together, gives its history and separates it from Santiago/Cape Verde Funaná. His own project expressly reinterprets Gumbé with this advertised band; a complete documented performing practice is used, not nationality-only classification. Existing funana describes the Santiago gaita/ferrinho dance practice. The broader cape_verdean_funana_maritime record covers Cape Verde maritime/emigration traditions including morna, coladeira, funaná and batuque, with guitar, cavaquinho and accordion; it is not limited to the gaita/ferrinho duo. Both overlap this cross-border project, but neither makes the separately documented Guinea-Bissau Gumbé field an alias. Broad African popular music and Lusophone diaspora fields overlap. No single homogeneous rhythm or universal instrumentation is asserted; the producer explicitly stresses Gumbé's internal stylistic diversity. Exact creator map not necessary or claimed for this directly named primary practice.

Producer Francisco Fininho Sousa's first-person account explicitly names modern Gumbé as a diverse Bissau musical field drawing several local traditions together, gives its history and separates it from Santiago/Cape Verde Funaná. Existing funana describes the Santiago gaita/ferrinho dance practice. The broader cape_verdean_funana_maritime record covers Cape Verde maritime/emigration traditions including morna, coladeira, funaná and batuque, with guitar, cavaquinho and accordion; it is not limited to the gaita/ferrinho duo. Both overlap this cross-border project, but neither makes the separately documented Guinea-Bissau Gumbé field an alias. Broad African popular music and Lusophone diaspora fields overlap. No single homogeneous rhythm or universal instrumentation is asserted; the producer explicitly stresses Gumbé's internal stylistic diversity. tradition.name: Haitian Traditional
tradition.lineage: Haitian traditional music — sacred and secular heritage spanning drum-song, dance and instrumental practice.

extras.description: Haitian traditional music includes ceremonial singing and tanbou drumming alongside secular dance, string music and bamboo-trumpet traditions. Call-and-response voices and interacting drum parts are central to many communal settings. Repertoire, ensemble and function vary across ceremonies, social dances and regional practices; Vodou drum-song is one prominent strand of this wider heritage.

tradition.name: Hyperpop Brasileiro
tradition.lineage: Hyperpop brasileiro connects Brazilian producers, DJs and pop artists through internet circulation, collaborations and events such as the Hyperpop Festival.

extras.description: Exaggerated electronic pop textures meet forceful dance rhythms and crossings with Brazilian funk, pagodão and other club styles. CyberKills exemplifies the DJ-led branch, where contrasting songs and sounds are shaped into continuous mixed programmes.

entries.geo_rationale: Issuer explicitly identifies Brazil; country-level editorial community anchor, not a claimed common birthplace, mixing room or performance site.
entries.neighbor_distinction: First-person CyberKills interviews document a Brazilian PC Music/hyperpop community, predecessors Mia Badgyal,Frimes,Léo Hainer and the duo-organized2020 Hyperpop Festival benefiting CUFA Mães da Favela. This is positive named national community evidence beyond birthplace; international festival guests do not become Brazilian by participation. The selected2025 programme is self-tagged hyperpop but openly crosses funk,pagodão baiano,Latin and electronic dance styles; no all-tracks-pure-hyperpop claim. Current creator membership of CyberKills is not independently established and is not asserted. Full existing hyperpop already spans global internet and queer production, so the Brazilian community is an overlapping regional branch rather than an excluded style. Hyperpop Rap focuses rap-form crossover and may overlap, but the national community includes broader pop/DJ and festival practice. Música Eletrônica Brasileira,Brazilian EDM and Eletrônica Underground Brasileira are wider overlapping national production/club fields; their selected KALOZIN,Pedro andCohen programmes do not delimit those entire fields. The positive hyperpop institution/community supplies the narrower boundary, not different equipment or merely a different set. Brazilian Experimental concerns a broader composition/experimentation field, not automatically all named hyperpop practice.

tradition.lineage: Hyperpop en Español is the Spanish-language community within the wider internet-era hyperpop field. Artists connect pop songwriting with electronic experimentation, drawing on club music, online collaboration and influences from several generations of pop.

extras.description: Bright electronic melodies, produced rhythms and digitally treated singing push pop hooks toward exaggerated textures. Rave influences and quick stylistic changes coexist with personal, song-centred expression.

entries.neighbor_distinction: Hyperpop en Español is the narrower Spanish-language hyperpop community within the full international hyperpop field. Rakky's firsthand Metal interview explicitly describes the need for this music in Spanish beyond UK/US English-language production, and identifies her music with hyperpop/bubblegum-bass while preferring the broad term pop. Her later ACERO interview candidly questions hyperpop's widened boundaries and changing scene; no rigid acoustic essence or exclusive self-label is imposed. University Granada and the event promoter independently locate her within the Spanish hyperpop network. The exact creator's full Hyperpop en Español playlist includes Rojuu,Fran Laoren,Orslok,Mda and many others; Rakky is not present in the current retrieved100 tracks, so her bridge relies on direct practitioner/institution evidence, not invented creator membership. Existing hyperpop already encompasses global queer/internet and maximalist electronic-pop practices; this is an overlapping language/community subset, not a new production technique or temporal exclusion. Hyperpop_rap is a rap-focused convergence, not the whole sung/pop/rave field; Spanish indie pop and Spanish pop rock retain wider/different scene scopes rather than being reduced to their particular exemplars. Existing German/French/Indonesian hyperpop are other national/language communities. The selected DJ programme deliberately crosses adjacent rave styles and is not claimed uniformly Spanish-language or exclusively hyperpop.

tradition.lineage: İlahiler are Turkish devotional songs setting religious and mystical poetry to composed melodies. They belong to mosque and tekke musical traditions as well as contemporary religious recordings, drawing on the makam and rhythmic practices of Turkish music.

extras.description: Solo and collective singing carry devotional poetry through melodic phrases and recurring rhythmic patterns. Both unaccompanied and instrumentally supported performances occur, with differing practices across religious settings and recording traditions.
exemplars: Sedat Uçan and Hasan Dursun — complete En Güzel Müziksiz İlahiler (2015)

tradition.name: Indie Boliviano
tradition.lineage: Indie Boliviano is Bolivia’s independent music community, connecting bands, labels and creative networks in cities including La Paz, Santa Cruz and Cochabamba. Its releases extend across alternative rock, electronic music and experimental approaches.

extras.description: Guitar-led songs may combine melodic vocals, bass and drums with synthesizer colour and programmed layers. Independent production also supports more electronic or exploratory arrangements beyond the band format.

entries.geo_rationale: Firsthand band interview identifies La Paz origin/community; city anchor, not recording-session location.
entries.neighbor_distinction: Indie Boliviano denotes the independent Bolivian label/festival/creative-community field spanning rock, electronic and experimental music. Songmess’s firsthand episode307 with Alfonso and Chuntu of Nuson explicitly describes that multi-city La Paz/Santa Cruz/Cochabamba field; Ciudad Líquida’s own interview expressly identifies indie/alternative practice and its independent local network. Exact EveryNoise artist membership not asserted. Full existing bolivian_rock already covers national rock beyond its Vadik Barrón exemplar and substantially overlaps this selected rock band; indie is not claimed to exclude rock or mainstream collaboration. The independent cross-style community extends beyond a rock-only label, positively evidenced by Nuson’s electronic/experimental field. Existing cumbia_boliviana, trap_boliviano, reggae_boliviano and jazz_boliviano cover stylistic national branches, not this cross-style production/community network. Pending Pop Boliviano is not presumed equivalent or resolved.

tradition.name: Indie Català
tradition.lineage: Indie Català connects independent labels, artists and festivals across Catalonia. Networks such as Bankrobber and popArb bring together pop, rock, folk, electronica and experimental approaches, with Catalan-language songwriting forming an important part of the scene.

extras.description: Lead singing interacts with clean electric guitar, bass and drums, while acoustic piano, keyboard and synthesizer layers broaden the harmonic color. Melodic vocal lines and contrasting instrumental textures support clear song structures within a stylistically varied independent field.

entries.geo_rationale: Editorial regional city anchor for explicitly documented surrounding Lleida villages, not exact Corbins studio coordinate or assertion all members live in city.
entries.neighbor_distinction: Indie Català is the Catalan independent-production and circulation community, positively defined by the actual popArb organizer as independent pop made in Catalonia and cross-artist connections, and the Bankrobber issuer explicitly tags this album indie català. Bankrobber identifies its independent label running since2002, spanning pop, electronica, folk, rock and experimental practice. Existing rock_catala is broad Catalan-language rock, not restricted to Sopa de Cabra or a historical date; this independent cross-style network overlaps it without claiming exclusivity. Existing musica_catalana is a broader cultural field, not limited to Gemma Humet piano/voice. Spanish indie pop and Spanish indie rock already encompass Catalan artists and Barcelona production, but do not exhaust the separately organized regional network. Nova Cançó scopes the protest-song lineage and Catalan folk traditional repertoire; neither is every modern Catalan independent production. Selected album exact creator membership is not asserted: current creator map retrieval failed, while positive issuer category and organizer practice independently support the bridge.
